Book Review: Architecture in the United States 
Architecture in the United States is an ambitious work and there are few writers as 
qualified to undertake such a project as Dell Upton, a distinguished scholar of 
American architectural history who, having a background in American studies, is as 
knowledgeable about vernacular architecture as about high style. The book is divided 
into five themes: Community, Nature, Technology, Money, and Art. The usefulness of 
this structure becomes apparent as one progresses through the book and realizes that 
Upton discusses not only houses, farms, and commercial buildings but also landscape 
architecture, gardens, bridges, public sculpture, and whole cities. His intention to 
examine architecture as an integral part of social and economic history. not primarily 
as a form of art, also fits well into these thematic divisions. 
The first chapter, ‘An American Icon’, is devoted to the house. Upton’s discussion of 
this elemental unit of architecture and its importance in relation to the primary social 
structure of the family is an effective introduction to the broad topic of architecture in 
relation to society. While much of the chapter focuses on examples of elite houses, 
including several presidential manors, Upton incorporates much essential information 
about common houses into his interpretations. This chapter, like the succeeding five, 
follows a loose chronological orientation in its analysis of several examples of homes 
from the seventeenth to the twentieth century, while integrating discussion of form 
and style with social and economic processes. 
Chapter 2, ‘Community’, examines monumental architecture ranging from Native 
American earthworks to state and federal capitols, memorials, monuments, and other 
public buildings, connecting them to issues such as planned communities, and other 
architectural definitions of community.  
In Chapter 3, ‘Nature’, Upton discusses the enormous influence of the wilderness, 
which was sometimes viewed as positive, sometimes negative, but always important, 
on the identity of the country. From first European settlement onwards, architecture 
‘was an ally against nature’. He contrasts this attitude, and its reflection in 
architecture, with that of Native Americans, who sought to live ‘in harmony with 
nature’. By the nineteenth century, this dynamic relationship between nature and 
culture was expressed in the creation of urban parks, suburban homes and 
movements such as Arts and Crafts, whose most notable product was the ubiquitous 
bungalow, a common type of American house. 
Chapter 4, ‘Technology’, starts with a description of different methods of construction, 
beginning with traditional timber framing and its evolution in the nineteenth century 
into the construction methods of balloon framing and prefabrication. Upton neglects 
some areas of special interest to the folk architecture scholar, such as why many 
farmers still built heavy, timber-frame, pegged barns well into the twentieth century.

11 
 
He moves quickly to discussion of industrial buildings and bridges, connecting 
Americans fascination with technology with their desire for structures of great size and 
scale. Finally, Upton analyzes several key movements in architecture and their 
connection to industrial design. 
Chapter 5, ‘Money’, segues naturally from the previous chapter: after an elaborate 
discussion of Pueblo Indian towns and their relationship to their society and economy, 
Upton describes the growth of major American cities and the role of commerce in that 
growth. This ‘cultural construction of economic life’ culminated in the skyscraper. 
From there he moves to an architectural interpretation of shopping malls and markets. 
The concluding chapter, ‘Art’, begins by examining the historical conception of 
architecture. American architecture as a profession began in the nineteenth century 
and, as the century progressed, the architect’s role became increasingly separate from 
that of the builder. Upton connects this progression to ‘the growing separation of 
head-work from handwork in all segments of the American economy’. However, 
architecture as a profession had inherited a special status, like art, from its role as a 
vehicle of social identity. ‘Architects claimed superiority to builders based on their 
taste, cultivated through special training, and immersion in architecture. The new 
architects were manufactured gentlemen who in tum needed to sell their tastes in a 
consumer economy.’ Upton continues with a discussion of the concept of style and its 
importance to the field of architecture: style is basically a visual vocabulary used to 
denote what is in vogue and was useful for claiming social place as well as 
contributing to professional standardization. Upton ends the chapter with the 
significant subtitle ‘Beyond Art’: ‘Every architect and every building belongs to several 
overlapping ‘high’ and ‘vernacular’ circles of architectural knowledge,’ he says. ‘These 
circles of architectural knowledge encompass technologies, social ideas, and meanings 
that are unaccounted for in, and often antagonistic to, art-architectural traditions.’ 
My only complaint about this masterful work is that it neglects one facet of American 
architecture that is essentially connected to American history, society, and economy, and 
that is the farmstead. The vast majority of built structures in this country until the 
twentieth century were of folk architectural origins, but the importance of the family 
farmstead to the construction of American society is often neglected nowadays. Architecture 
in the United States has a bias toward the urban and elite over the rural or folk in terms of 
its coverage, but the fact that this book includes any discussion of folk architecture at all is 
a testament to the tremendous progress that field has made in the past thirty years. In this 
beautifully written and illustrated book, Upton displays his commanding expertise in all 
areas of architecture.
